L0@P0: CANCV-4—
L1@P0: Canine Autologous
L2@P0: Nanoparticle Cancer
L3@P0: Vaccine (V4)
L4@P0: Immunotherapy For Dogs
L5@P0: Dr Chris Weir
L6@P0: Principal Scientist | Dog Oncology Group Pty Ltd.
L7@P0: e. dr.c.w@outlook.com
L8@P0: C&T No. 6027
L9@P0: Some cancers produce unique proteins or antigens on
L10@P0: their surface which differ from that of a normal cell.
L11@P0: These proteins can provide a target for the immune
L12@P0: system. CANCV-4 utilises the dog’s own cancer tissue to
L13@P0: produce a vaccine which ‘re-educates’ and stimulates
L14@P0: the immune system so it recognises and targets the
L15@P0: cancer.
L16@P0: The Evolution: CACV-1—CANCV-4
L17@P0: Over a period of 7 years CANCV has been tested, refined,
L18@P0: and improved to increase levels of immune stimulation
L19@P0: and response:
L20@P0: CACV-1 Used a commercially available adjuvant—
L21@P0: immunity waned over time and no
L22@P0: apparent response in tumour types like
L23@P0: Melanoma. Results of this initial cohort
L24@P0: were published Vet. Sci. 2018, 5(4), 87;
L25@P0: doi.org/10.3390/vetsci5040087
L26@P0: CANCV-2 Nanoparticle adjuvant was introduced
L27@P0: to replace commercially available one
L28@P0: after increased efficacy was seen in
L29@P0: rodent cancer models.
L30@P0: CANCV-3 Higher dose nanoparticles and
L31@P0: improved cancer protein isolation and
L32@P0: extraction. Introduction of immune
L33@P0: stimulant into the vaccine to draw more
L34@P0: immune cells into the vaccination site.
L35@P0: CANCV-4 Further modified nanoparticles for
L36@P0: increased immune stimulation with
L37@P0: improved dendritic cell uptake and
L38@P0: antigen presentation to T cells.
L39@P0: Incorporation of tumour antigens into or
L40@P0: onto the nanoparticle for slower release
L41@P0: and improved immune cell uptake.
L42@P0: Ability to use fresh, frozen, formalin
L43@P0: fixed or paraffin embedded tumour
L44@P0: tissue.
L45@P0: The Process
L46@P0: Fresh or frozen tissue is collected and sent to the lab for
L47@P0: processing. Formalin fixed, paraffin embedded tissue
L48@P0: can also be used to make a vaccine, but this takes longer
L49@P0: to process (4 days). The process involves:
L50@P0: 1. Processing the tissue to a singular protein level.
L51@P0: 2. Treating the proteins to expose
L52@P0: more potential antigens.
L53@P0: 3. Combining with or incorporating the antigens
L54@P0: into the nanoparticles with immune stimulant.
L55@P0: 4. Bottling for administration.
L56@P0: CANCV-4 DOSING SCHEDULE
L57@P0: Initial doses (0.4 mL) are given intramuscularly 4 x weekly,
L58@P0: 2 x weekly and 2 x fortnightly or 4 x fortnightly and then
L59@P0: four monthly boosters are administered. Depending on
L60@P0: your dog’s cancer scenario and sample size, more doses
L61@P0: can be made and administered after initial course.
L62@P0: Safety
L63@P0: Various versions of CANCV have been used to treat over
L64@P0: 700 dogs with different types of cancer. Minor, temporary
L65@P0: side-effects, lasting 24-48 hours may occur, such as
L66@P0: lumps at the vaccination site, malaise, fatigue, or loss of
L67@P0: appetite. No major side effects or anaphylaxis seen.
L68@P0: Scenarios for Use
L69@P0: Primary treatment—following tumour removal by surgery
L70@P0: (clean/narrow/dirty margins)—to prevent or slow tumour
L71@P0: regrowth.
L72@P0: Combined with standard of care treatments (e.g.
L73@P0: chemotherapy)—particularly single agent chemotherapy.
L74@P0: As an accessory to debulking large tumours—to aid
L75@P0: regression, ‘stabilise the tumour’ or slow tumour
L76@P0: regrowth.
L77@P0: Figure 1. 0.2g of fresh, Paraffin embedded, or
L78@P0: formalin fixed tissue is required for an initial
L79@P0: eight dose course of vaccine
L80@P0: Normal cell surface
L81@P0: antigen
L82@P0: Cancer associated
L83@P0: antigen
L84@P0: Vaccine made specifically
L85@P0: for that patient
L86@P0-1: Centre for Veterinary Education | Est. 1965 Celebrating 55 years of publication in 2024 Page 27As part of palliative care—In dogs with advanced disease
L87@P1: combining the vaccine with prednisone can in some
L88@P1: cases improve expected survival.
L89@P1: The publication (see below) from 2018 reported initial
L90@P1: data obtained from CACV-1 which incorporated a
L91@P1: commercially available adjuvant. This study between
L92@P1: 2016-2018 was designed to show safety and look for
L93@P1: evidence of efficacy with the CACV-1 vaccine formulation.
L94@P1: The study also compared the relative response rates
L95@P1: of adding an extra stimulant (Rhizavidin) to the vaccine
L96@P1: versus without. At the time of publication, dogs receiving
L97@P1: Rhizavidin in their vaccine had lower survival rates (50%)
L98@P1: compared to dogs receiving vaccine without it (75%). By
L99@P1: 2019, all dogs with vaccine formulated with rhizavidin
L100@P1: were deceased and approximately 20% of those not
L101@P1: receiving it remained alive. One key observation from
L102@P1: the study was that weekly vaccinations to start appeared
L103@P1: to improve survival and this practice has been followed
L104@P1: with CANCV-2 to 4 or with slight variations. The study
L105@P1: highlighted also that the age of a dog effects efficacy of
L106@P1: this autologous vaccine approach with dogs greater than
L107@P1: >12 years of age less likely to gain benefit.
L108@P1: By the end of 2019, CACV-1 was being phased out after
L109@P1: the remaining dogs relapsed. Many of these were
L110@P1: switched to CANCV-2/3 and a proportion of these dogs
L111@P1: remain alive today.
L112@P1: Disclaimer
L113@P1: While we have seen excellent results when treating
L114@P1: dogs with CANCV2-4 we cannot guarantee that this
L115@P1: treatment will be effective for all dogs. While every
L116@P1: effort is made to obtain the best outcome, there
L117@P1: can be many factors that have an impact on the
L118@P1: effectiveness of the vaccine. Variables may include
L119@P1: how advanced the cancer is, what type of cancer,
L120@P1: age of the dog, the level of disease, prior treatments
L121@P1: for the cancer, as well as the quality of the tumour
L122@P1: sample used to create the vaccine. For best
L123@P1: potential outcomes, the full course of recommended
L124@P1: vaccinations must be completed.
L125@P1: Cases and Testimonials
L126@P1: Dr Michaela Swan BVSc Hons MANZCVS (Small Animal
L127@P1: Medicine)
L128@P1: Oncology Registrar
L129@P1: I have used autologous vaccines created by Dr Weir
L130@P1: since 2020. The process of submitting tumour samples,
L131@P1: receiving the vaccines, and communicating with Dr Weir
L132@P1: has always been easy. I have used the vaccines for a wide
L133@P1: variety of cancers in both cats and dogs. The vaccines
L134@P1: are well tolerated, and I have not seen any side effects
L135@P1: of the vaccines. These personalised vaccines harness
L136@P1: the patient’s immune system to attack their cancer.
L137@P1: Thus, this is another form of treatment in addition to
L138@P1: more traditional therapies for cancers such as surgery,
L139@P1: chemotherapy, and radiation. The lack of side effects
L140@P1: and possibility of a benefit from these vaccines entices
L141@P1: owners to elect this therapy, often in addition to other
L142@P1: more traditional treatments. Anecdotally, I have seen
L143@P1: improved survival times in dogs with osteosarcomas
L144@P1: who have had amputations, chemotherapy, and ongoing
L145@P1: autologous vaccine therapy.
L146@P1: Immunotherapy is rapidly growing field and it is becoming
L147@P1: a huge component of therapy for a number of human
L148@P1: cancers. With ongoing research like Dr Weir’s, hopefully
L149@P1: it can have a similar role in veterinary medicine.
L150@P1: Dr Fiona Coghill BVSc MANZCVS
L151@P1: MVM DECVS EBVS European
L152@P1: Specialist in Small Animal
L153@P1: Surgery
L154@P1: Brindabella Veterinary Referral
L155@P1: Service, Canberra
L156@P1: Floki, an 8-year-old Dogue de Bordeaux cross
L157@P1: who is full of life, 4 months after treatment with
L158@P1: mandibulectomy and CANCV-4 for stage 3 oral
L159@P1: malignant melanoma
L160@P1: I use Canine Autologous Nanoparticle Cancer Vaccine
L161@P1: V4 ( CANCV-4) in my patients after oncological surgery.
L162@P1: It is well tolerated by patients and is easily combined
L163@P1: with conventional chemotherapy protocols. Having the
L164@P1: vaccine made is as easy as posting a frozen sample of the
L165@P1: tumour to Dr Chris Weir at Dog Oncology Group (DOG).
L166@P1: The vaccine is made quickly, usually having it back in time
L167@P1: for the first post-surgical recheck. In my experience,
L168@P1: owners are excited to consider CANCV-4 due to the
L169@P1: safety aspect of a vaccine created from their dog’s own
L170@P1: tissue and the knowledge that immunotherapy is an
L171@P1: additional weapon in the fight against their dog’s cancer.
L172@P1: My current osteosarcoma and oral malignant melanoma
L173@P1: cases are surviving beyond expected median survival
L174@P1: times using the combination of surgery, chemotherapy
L175@P1: and CANCV-4.
L176@P1: More case reports and testimonials.
L177@P1: Cancer Types: Resources
L178@P1: akcchf.org
L179@P1: acfoundation.org/
L180@P1: Read the 2018 study here.
L181@P1-2: Page 28 Control & Therapy Series – Issue 315 June 2024 Authors’ views are not necessarily those of the CVELymphoma In early 2020, a phase 2 placebo trial of CANCV-2 (version 2) combined with CHOP for
L182@P2: Multicentric B and T-cell lymphoma was commenced just as the Covid-19 pandemic started
L183@P2: which severely affected the study. The aim of the study was to see if adding vaccine to CHOP
L184@P2: or palliative care extends survival. Of the 28 dogs recruited, 4 died prior to receiving the
L185@P2: vaccine or placebo vaccine (adjuvant only); of the remaining 24, 13 received the vaccine and
L186@P2: 11 the placebos. The results were inconclusive due to low recruitment with median survival
L187@P2: times of 10-11 months in both groups. Despite this, the trial produced some important
L188@P2: observations:
L189@P2: 1. That vaccination with adjuvant only can have an immune boosting benefit on its own
L190@P2: 2. Only 20-25% of dogs probably benefit from the addition of vaccine or adjuvant with CHOP
L191@P2: 3. Single agent Dox + vaccine could be another cheaper treatment option
L192@P2: 4. Boosting with adjuvant prior to surgery and treatment may
L193@P2: be another option to improve survival times
L194@P2: 5. While palliative, prednisone is immunosuppressive; approximately
L195@P2: 10-15% dogs will have a significant extension of survival with the
L196@P2: addition of vaccine over prednisone alone (4-6 weeks)
L197@P2: Haemangiosarcoma Dogs with haemangiosarcoma survive between 30-90 days if treated with surgery alone.
L198@P2: Standard of care surgery and chemotherapy (Doxorubicin) improves average survival to 6
L199@P2: months. If the cancer has not spread to other parts of the body (metastasized), evidence
L200@P2: indicates that treatment with CANCV-2/3 can improve survival times, with some dogs
L201@P2: surviving for more than 2 years. No dogs have been treated with CANCV-4 yet.
L202@P2: Mast cell tumours
L203@P2: (MCT)
L204@P2: A.
L205@P2: C.
L206@P2: B.
L207@P2-3: Centre for Veterinary Education | Est. 1965 Celebrating 55 years of publication in 2024 Page 29Mast cell tumours
L208@P3: (MCT) continued
L209@P3: Nearly 200 dogs have been treated for both high and low grade MCT with vaccine alone
L210@P3: or with chemotherapy (CCNU, Vincristine) or palladia. Figure A Shows the significant lower
L211@P3: rate of recurrence in dogs with low grade treated with CANCV-2-4 compared to CACV-1
L212@P3: which vaccine formulation has now been abandoned. Figure B shows that no dogs with
L213@P3: recurring low grade MCT have recurred again after CANCV-2-4 treatment compared to CACV1. Figure C compares the outcomes of high grade MCTs treated with CACV-1 v CANCV2-4
L214@P3: alone or with CCNU/Palladia/Vincristine—Demonstrating a significant extension of survival.
L215@P3: (Data collected 2017-2023)
L216@P3: Melanoma CACV-1 showed no efficacy against melanoma, and this was a driver to switch to a
L217@P3: nanoparticle adjuvant. CANCV-2 to CANCV-4 have demonstrated they can slow progression,
L218@P3: reduce metastatic disease, and extend survival in some dogs with melanoma.
L219@P3: Osteosarcoma Standard therapy of amputation and treatment with chemotherapy (Carbo/Cisplatin), gives
L220@P3: a median survival time of 11 months with 20% of dogs surviving for over 2 years. Seventy dogs
L221@P3: have been treated with a combination of carboplatin and CANCV-2 to-4. Dogs treated with
L222@P3: CANCV-3 and carboplatin have a median survival of 14 months with 30% of dogs surviving
L223@P3: to 31 months. Currently 19 dogs have been treated with CANCV-4 and carboplatin. These
L224@P3: results will take another 18-24 months to fully obtain and see if there is an improvement on
L225@P3: CANCV-3.
L226@P3: Soft tissue sarcoma These tumours recur in approximately 20% of dogs after surgery alone, with metastatic
L227@P3: spread to other tissues occurring in 25%. CANCV-4 has successfully stopped recurrence and
L228@P3: slowed regrowth in dogs with high grade residual tumour.
L229@P3: Carcinoma (various
L230@P3: types and tumour

L232@P3: CANCV-4. can potentially stabilise disease, prolong survival or prevent recurrence. Combined
